summary: Describes the entryUUID operational attribute, with its matching rules and syntax. It holds a server-assigned Universally Unique Identifier for an object, which clients can use to tell objects apart or find one after renaming. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Every entry gets a permanent serial number, so you can find it even if its name changes.

questions: why are ldap distinguished names not stable identifiers
what is an operational attribute in ldap
subtitle: A permanent, server-assigned serial number for every LDAP directory entry, so clients can find an entry even after it is renamed.

tldr.problem: An LDAP entry is identified by its distinguished name, but names are not stable: a new object can later get a name that once belonged to another object that was renamed or deleted.
tldr.mechanism: The server assigns each entry a UUID when it is added and exposes it as the read-only, single-valued 'entryUUID' operational attribute. The RFC also defines the UUID syntax and two matching rules, 'uuidMatch' and 'uuidOrderingMatch'.
tldr.outcome: Clients can tell objects apart and locate an entry after renaming. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 4530 is a Proposed Standard from June 2006, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Names Are Not Enough
sections.content:
In X.500 directory services, including those reached through the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP), an object is identified by its distinguished name (DN). The RFC points out that DNs are not stable identifiers: a new object may be identified by a DN that previously identified another object that has since been renamed or deleted.

A Universally Unique Identifier (UUID) is, quoting RFC 4122, an identifier unique across both space and time. RFC 4530 defines the entryUUID operational attribute, which holds the UUID the server assigned to an entry. Clients can use it to distinguish the objects a particular DN has identified, or to locate a particular object after it has been renamed.
sections.plainLanguage: A name on a mailbox can be painted over and given to a new family. A serial number stamped on the mailbox itself never gets reused for someone else.

sections.title: The UUID Syntax
sections.content:
A UUID is a 16-octet (128-bit) value. The RFC defines the ASN.1 type as UUID ::= OCTET STRING (SIZE(16)), constrained to a UUID as described in RFC 4122.

On the wire in LDAP, values are not sent as raw octets. They use the ASCII character string representation from RFC 4122, for example 597ae2f6-16a6-1027-98f4-d28b5365dc14. The syntax is registered with the object identifier 1.3.6.1.1.16.1 and the description 'UUID', in a form suitable for publication in subschema subentries.
sections.plainLanguage: The serial number is a long code of 16 bytes. When it is written down for people and computers to swap, it is spelled out as letters and digits separated by dashes.

sections.title: The Two Matching Rules
sections.content:
A matching rule tells a server how to compare values. RFC 4530 defines two for UUIDs.

  • uuidMatch (1.3.6.1.1.16.2) checks an asserted UUID against a stored one for equality. Its semantics are the same as octetStringMatch, except that the assertion value is written in the UUID string form rather than the normal octet string form.
  • uuidOrderingMatch (1.3.6.1.1.16.3) compares for ordering, in the same way as octetStringOrderingMatch, again with the UUID string form for the assertion.

The RFC adds a caution about ordering: not all UUID variants have a defined ordering, and even where one exists, servers are not obligated to assign UUIDs in any particular order. The ordering rule is provided for completeness.
sections.plainLanguage: One rule asks 'is this the same serial number?'. The other asks 'which comes first?', but the second one is only there to be complete, because serial numbers are not handed out in any special order.

sections.title: The entryUUID Attribute
sections.content:
The entryUUID attribute (1.3.6.1.1.16.4) provides the UUID assigned to the entry. Its definition uses uuidMatch for equality, uuidOrderingMatch for ordering and the UUID syntax, and it is marked SINGLE-VALUE, NO-USER-MODIFICATION and USAGE directoryOperation. That last flag makes it an operational attribute: one the server maintains for its own purposes rather than ordinary user data.

The server requirements are short and firm. Servers SHALL generate and assign a new UUID to each entry when it is added to the directory and provide it as the value of entryUUID. An entry's UUID is immutable. UUIDs are to be generated in accordance with Section 4 of RFC 4122, and servers MUST ensure each generated UUID is unique in space and time.

Because the attribute is NO-USER-MODIFICATION, clients can read it and search on it but cannot change it.
sections.plainLanguage: The directory stamps a number on each new entry when it is created. Nobody can change it afterward, and the directory must make sure no two entries ever get the same number.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An entry's relative distinguished name (RDN) is built from attribute values of the entry, which are commonly descriptive of the object. The RFC encourages naming attributes whose values are widely disclosable, but notes that entries are often named using information that cannot be disclosed to all parties.

A UUID carries no descriptive information about the object it identifies, so it can be used to point at a particular entry without revealing its contents. The general security considerations of RFC 4122 and RFC 4510 (LDAP) also apply.
sections.plainLanguage: A serial number does not say anything about what the thing is, so you can talk about 'item 597...' without telling everyone what is inside.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The IANA registered the values this document specifies, following the LDAP registration procedures in RFC 4520. There is an object identifier registration identifying the UUID schema elements, a syntax registration (1.3.6.1.1.16.1), two matching rule descriptors (uuidMatch as 1.3.6.1.1.16.2 and uuidOrderingMatch as 1.3.6.1.1.16.3), and an attribute type descriptor (entryUUID as 1.3.6.1.1.16.4). The change controller for each is the IESG.
sections.plainLanguage: The new names and numbers were written into an official public list so nobody else uses them for something different.
